claim: OHLC definitions of open, close, high, low.

edits.old: A price chart is a record of past trades. The most common style is the candlestick chart. Each candle summarises one slice of time - a minute, a day, a week - with four numbers. The open is the first trade of the period. The close is the last trade. The high is the most anyone paid during the period, and the low is the least. Those four numbers are often shortened to OHLC.

The open is the first trade of the period. The close is the last trade. The high is the most anyone paid during the period, and the low is the least. Those four numbers are often shortened to OHLC.

claim: Up/down candle coloring description vs how the app draws candles.

edits.old: The body shows where the period started and finished. If the close is above the open, the candle is an up candle and is usually drawn hollow or in a lighter colour. If the close is below the open, it is a down candle and is usually drawn filled or in a darker colour. The wicks show how far trading strayed from the body before coming back. A long wick means the price visited that level but did not stay there.
edits.new: The body shows where the period started and finished. If the close is above the open, the candle is an up candle; if the close is below the open, it is a down candle. Color conventions vary between charting tools. In this app's charts, up candles are blue and down candles are amber. The wicks show how far trading strayed from the body before coming back. A long wick means the price visited that level but did not stay there.

note: App fills both: up = Econ.sky (blue), down = Econ.amber; nothing hollow. Text said hollow/lighter vs filled/darker, which does not match. Also fixed "colour". Lead removed an unverified reference to the diagram's body color.

claim: Weekly candle construction: Monday open, Friday close, five days.

edits.old: Timeframe is the length of time each candle covers. A weekly candle is not a new set of facts; it is five daily candles squeezed into one. Its open is Monday's open, its close is Friday's close, and its high and low are the highest high and lowest low of the whole week. That is why a choppy week of daily candles can become a single calm-looking weekly candle.
edits.new: Timeframe is the length of time each candle covers. A weekly candle is not a new set of facts; it is that week's daily candles, usually five, squeezed into one. Its open is the first trading day's open, its close is the last trading day's close, and its high and low are the highest high and lowest low of the whole week. That is why a choppy week of daily candles can become a single calm-looking weekly candle.

note: Holiday weeks have fewer than five sessions and may not start Monday or end Friday; changed to first/last trading day.

claim: Support is past summary; lines break and get redrawn.

edits.old: A support line is a summary of past turns. It says the price turned here before; it does not say the price must turn here again. Prices break through support and resistance all the time, and when they do, chart readers simply redraw the lines. Treat these lines as a way to organise what you see, not as a barrier that the market has agreed to respect.

claim: Doji and hammer definitions.

edits.old: Three common candle shapes show how the vocabulary works. A doji has an open and close that are almost equal, so the body is a thin line and the wicks do the talking; it describes a period that ended where it began. A hammer has a small body near the top and a long lower wick and appears after a decline; it describes a period in which the price fell hard, then recovered most of the drop before the close.
edits.new: Three common candle shapes show how the vocabulary works. A doji has an open and close that are almost equal, so the body is a thin line and the wicks do the talking; it describes a period that ended where it began. A hammer appears after a decline and has a small body near the top of its range, a lower wick at least about twice as long as the body, and little or no upper wick; it describes a period in which the price fell hard, then recovered most of the drop before the close.

note: Hammer definition lacked the standard lower-wick >= ~2x body and little/no upper-wick criteria. Doji definition correct.

claim: Lo, Mamaysky & Wang (NBER w7613, Mar 2000): patterns, 1962-1996, incremental information.

edits.old: Researchers have tested whether these shapes say anything about what happens next. In a National Bureau of Economic Research working paper issued in March 2000, Andrew Lo, Harry Mamaysky, and Jiang Wang used a computer method to detect classic chart patterns in U.S. stock prices from 1962 to 1996 and asked whether the days after a pattern differed statistically from ordinary days. They reported that several patterns carried some incremental information. They did not claim the patterns made money.
edits.new: Researchers have tested whether chart shapes say anything about what happens next. In a National Bureau of Economic Research working paper issued in March 2000, Andrew Lo, Harry Mamaysky, and Jiang Wang used a computer method to detect classic multi-day chart patterns, such as head-and-shoulders and double bottoms, in U.S. stock prices from 1962 to 1996 and asked whether the days after a pattern differed statistically from ordinary days. They reported that several patterns carried some incremental information and may have some practical value. Their test did not cover single-candle shapes such as the hammer, and it measured statistical differences, not profits after trading costs.

note: Authors/date/sample correct, but "these shapes" implied doji/hammer/engulfing were tested; w7613 studied head-and-shoulders, double-bottoms etc. Also abstract says "may have some practical value"; added for fairness.

claim: Trading-rule effects small, unstable, vanish after costs or publication; evidence "mixed at best".

edits.old: A pattern can shift the odds a little and still be useless in practice, because acting on it costs money: commissions, the spread between buying and selling prices, and taxes. Tests of trading rules across many markets have found effects that are small, unstable from period to period, and that often shrink or vanish after costs or after publication. The honest summary is that the evidence on forecasting power is mixed at best, which makes patterns fine for reading a chart and poor as a reason to act.
edits.new: A pattern can shift the odds a little and still be useless in practice, because acting on it costs money: commissions, the spread between buying and selling prices, and taxes. The wider evidence cuts both ways. Research on simple trading rules in currency markets found some predictive value, but one study found it shrank sharply once periods of central bank intervention were set aside. A study of many stock-return patterns found that few high-turnover strategies stayed statistically significant after trading costs. That makes patterns fine for reading a chart and a weak reason to act.

note: Original claims (esp. "after publication") had no cited source. Rewritten to what NBER w5505 (LeBaron 1996) and w20721 (Novy-Marx & Velikov 2014) state; both added to sources.

claim: SEC day trading extremely risky; FINRA losses; SEC pump-and-dump by "insiders".

edits.old: The SEC's investor education site describes day trading - rapid buying and selling within one day to catch short moves - as extremely risky and able to produce large losses very quickly. FINRA adds that frequent intraday trading, especially on borrowed money, can end in losing some or all of what was put in. The SEC also warns of pump-and-dump schemes, where false hype lifts a price before insiders sell. A chart never tells you why the price moved.
edits.new: The SEC's investor education site describes day trading - rapid buying and selling within one day to catch short moves - as extremely risky and able to produce large losses very quickly. FINRA adds that frequent intraday trading, especially on borrowed money, can end in losing some or all of what was put in. The SEC also warns of pump-and-dump schemes, where fraudsters spread false or misleading hype to lift a price, then sell their own shares. A chart never tells you why the price moved.

note: Day trading ("extremely risky... substantial financial losses in a very short period") and FINRA verified. SEC says "fraudsters", not insiders, sell at the inflated price.
